title: The Arrival Lists
passage:
Kelvain is nineteen years old and has a list. Ninety hectares of black tephra at the northern end of the Sarnhold Rise, still steaming at two vents, and a cumulative record of everything found on it since the sea stopped boiling: sixty-one vascular plants, forty-odd invertebrates, nine breeding birds. The list is reissued after every summer survey, and it has never once been shorter than the year before. That is not a compliment to Kelvain. A cumulative list is a ratchet. It registers arrivals and has no way at all of registering departures, so the figure that reaches the newspapers each autumn is a count of everything the island has ever held rather than of anything it holds now.

Ilse Draeven has been going out to the Rise for nineteen summers, to Kelvain and to six younger islands around it, and she counts differently: not what is new, but what is still there. On the question of arrival her surveys support the textbook almost exactly. Spores and dust-fine seeds came first, carried on the wind within a season or two of the ground cooling; drift-line plants followed, thrown up on the strandline in mats of weed; the bird-carried species arrived last and slowest. That sequence held on six of the seven islands, and the totals recorded in the first decade sat close to what had been forecast for ground of that age and that distance from the mainland. Draeven says this part of the record is not in dispute. New islands are colonized in roughly the order and at roughly the pace the textbooks give.

What nineteen years show, and one year cannot, is how much of that leaves again. Of the sixty-one plant species on Kelvain's list, nineteen were found in each of the last three surveys. The rest are gone, some of them after a single season: the median stay for a wind-arrived plant on Kelvain works out at a little over three years, and for the fine-seeded composites that crowd the early lists it is shorter still. The standing flora of the island has not grown since about its twelfth year. The published number has grown every year. Both of those are true, and only one of them is ever printed, because a ratchet cannot report a loss even when the loss is most of what has happened.

Why anything stays is a harder question than why anything comes, and it is here that Draeven and the volcanologists part company. Petar Ruhe, who has mapped the Rise since before Kelvain existed, holds that the biology is downstream of the rock and always will be. Fresh tephra is loose, and waves take it. An island outlives its eruption only if the ash is hot and fine enough to react with seawater and set into palagonite, and that is settled in the first months, by nothing that later flies in. "An island turns to rock in its first winter, or it is a shoal with a name," Ruhe says. "Vessa had eleven species. Vessa is a depth sounding." Draeven grants him the half of it she thinks is his: nothing colonizes a shoal, and an uncemented island never gets an ecology to lose. But cementation is a fact about the shore rather than the surface. Kelvain's rim is armored and its interior is still largely bare tephra, and almost every one of the nineteen surviving plants stands inside the two hectares under the petrel colony, on ground the birds have been manuring for a decade. Petrels make soil faster than weather does. Petrels are also tenants. When a storm took the headland off Odren's south cape, the colony there moved to a stack four kilometers away, and the plants its nitrogen had been feeding thinned by half within four seasons. Odren's published list did not move at all.

So an island is reported as an event. It surfaces, it is named, it is counted, and the counting is done with an instrument that cannot run backward. Draeven would like the arrival list printed beside two other things: a median residence time, and the name of whatever is currently supplying the island's nitrogen. The second is usually a colony of birds with better options elsewhere. She will not say what Kelvain will look like at fifty. What she will say is that the island is not finished, that nothing standing on it is safe, and that the only number anyone remembers about the place is the one that was never able to fall.
— Nadia Berthold

tephra = the loose ash and rock fragments thrown out by a volcanic eruption
palagonite = the tough rock that forms when hot volcanic ash reacts with seawater

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: That seabird colonies turn out to be the one thing keeping any plant alive on new volcanic ground.
That whether an island lasts at all is settled in its first months, when its tephra either sets or does not.
That the figure by which new islands are judged can only climb, and so reports nothing that is lost.
That new islands are now reached far faster than they once were, by species traveling routes that are new.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text gist), edge position 1. WHY-KEY (C): the ratchet is the spine of the piece and returns in three of the five paragraphs. Paragraph 1 introduces it — 'A cumulative list is a ratchet. It registers arrivals and has no way at all of registering departures' — paragraph 3 gives it a number ('Of the sixty-one plant species on Kelvain's list, nineteen were found in each of the last three surveys... The published number has grown every year'), paragraph 4 closes the Odren story on it ('Odren's published list did not move at all'), and the verdict names it a last time ('the only number anyone remembers about the place is the one that was never able to fall'). C paraphrases that without reusing a run of the passage's wording. WHY-NOT-A (trap: scope_error / detail-as-main, distorted): the petrel colony is the passage's most concrete cause and a blind reader who fixes on paragraph 4 will reach for it, but the text makes it a sub-point of the stay-versus-arrive question, and 'the one thing' is a distortion — the same paragraph makes cementation a precondition ('an uncemented island never gets an ecology to lose'), so the colony is not offered as the sole agent. WHY-NOT-B (trap: role_or_attribution_swap promoted to thesis): this is Ruhe's quoted position, given in his own voice ('An island turns to rock in its first winter, or it is a shoal with a name'), and it is real material rather than an invention — which is what makes it tempting. But the writer grants it only 'the half of it she thinks is his' and then spends the rest of the paragraph on what cementation does not settle, and the piece is not organized around island survival at all. WHY-NOT-D (trap: outside_knowledge): accelerating dispersal along new routes is the most familiar public story about colonization and reads as topical, so a passage-blind solver will consider it seriously. The text says the opposite of novelty — arrivals came 'in roughly the order and at roughly the pace the textbooks give' — and never discusses rates changing over historical time.

questions.prompt: What does the text say about the arrivals recorded in Draeven's surveys?

options.text: They were too irregular from island to island for any predicted sequence to be read into them.
The bird-carried species reached every one of the seven islands before the drift-line plants got there.
Most of what the early surveys logged had already gone again by the time of the survey after it.
They came in the expected order on nearly every island, in totals close to those forecast.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 2. WHY-KEY (D): 'That sequence held on six of the seven islands, and the totals recorded in the first decade sat close to what had been forecast for ground of that age and that distance from the mainland.' D recasts six-of-seven as 'nearly every island' and 'sat close to what had been forecast' as 'close to those forecast' — paraphrase, not lift. WHY-NOT-A (trap: over-hedged contradiction): built deliberately as the cautious-sounding wrong answer, because a test-wise student who reaches for the measured option should not be rewarded here. It is contradicted head-on: the sequence held on six of the seven islands and Draeven says 'this part of the record is not in dispute'. WHY-NOT-B (trap: quantifier_upgrade plus order reversal): every element of it is drawn from the passage's own vocabulary — bird-carried species, drift-line plants, the seven islands — and the seven is exact, which makes it feel checked. But the passage puts the bird-carried species last ('the bird-carried species arrived last and slowest'), and the sequence held on six islands, not all seven. WHY-NOT-C (trap: wrong_location, shifted in time): the turnover finding belongs to paragraph 3 and to nineteen years, not to the arrivals record; and even there the passage gives a median stay of 'a little over three years' for wind-arrived plants, so 'most... by the survey after it' overstates the loss rate as well. A reader who has finished the piece and remembers turnover as its news accepts it too quickly.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the plant species recorded on Kelvain?

options.text: Sixty-one have been logged in all, but under a third showed up in the three most recent surveys.
The earliest arrivals thinned out as the species that came after them proved better competitors for the same ground.
Each species that reaches the island holds on for a little over three years before dropping out of the record.
The count fell in several years of the record, recovering each time a new group of arrivals came ashore.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 3. WHY-KEY (A): 'Of the sixty-one plant species on Kelvain's list, nineteen were found in each of the last three surveys.' Nineteen of sixty-one is under a third, and A states the arithmetic rather than the sentence. This is the unit's deliberate hedge inversion (law 10): here the key is the flat, numerically confident claim and the option built to sound careful (C, with its 'a little over three years') is wrong, so 'choose the qualified answer' scores nothing across this unit. WHY-NOT-B (trap: outside_knowledge / plausible mechanism never stated): competitive displacement is the textbook explanation a reader brings to any account of falling species numbers, and the passage does report early arrivals disappearing, so the story fits the shape of the evidence. The text never mentions competition; it attributes persistence to soil made by the petrels and to nothing else. WHY-NOT-C (trap: quantifier_upgrade): the figure is genuine but doubly scoped in the passage — it is a median, and it is a median for wind-arrived plants only ('the median stay for a wind-arrived plant on Kelvain works out at a little over three years'). C promotes a median to a uniform term and a subset to all arrivals. WHY-NOT-D (trap: surface_word_match on the passage's counting language): 'count', 'record' and 'arrivals' are all the passage's own words, and a reader who has absorbed that the flora shrinks may assume the number followed it down. It is precisely what the passage rules out: the list 'has never once been shorter than the year before', which is the whole reason the ratchet matters.

questions.prompt: Almost all of Kelvain's surviving plants grow under its petrel colony. What does the Odren episode suggest about that?

options.text: A storm that takes a headland will drive off the colony nesting there and leave the plants below it to die.
What survives on Kelvain now is held there by an occupant with somewhere else it can go.
Colonies on new islands would need protection from disturbance before their plants could be expected to persist.
Nitrogen once delivered into the ground stays there, so a colony's departure costs an island very little.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 4. The passage sets two facts side by side and declines to join them: 'almost every one of the nineteen surviving plants stands inside the two hectares under the petrel colony', and, four sentences later, the Odren colony 'moved to a stack four kilometers away, and the plants its nitrogen had been feeding thinned by half within four seasons'. The stem restates the first fact so that the item asks for the join rather than for either fact; it does not entail which join. WHY-KEY (B): Odren establishes that a petrel colony is mobile and that its departure costs the ground under it; Kelvain's standing flora is concentrated under exactly such a colony; so what is left on Kelvain is being held by a tenant that has alternatives — which is the inch the reader has to walk. The verdict confirms it obliquely, calling the island's nitrogen source 'usually a colony of birds with better options elsewhere'. WHY-NOT-A (trap: too_literal, with two planted flaws): it restates the Odren sentence, which is retrieval rather than implication, and a solver who wants firm ground takes it. Its flaws are the generalization 'will' — the passage reports one storm at one cape, not a rule — and 'to die', where the passage says the plants 'thinned by half within four seasons'. WHY-NOT-C (trap: too_far): a two-step leap out of ecology into policy. The text prescribes nothing, and Draeven's own recommendation is about what should be published beside the arrival list, not about how colonies should be managed. WHY-NOT-D (trap: outside_knowledge, contradicted): soil nitrogen persisting after its source is removed is a defensible-sounding piece of general knowledge and would neatly explain why an island might not miss its birds, which is what makes it dangerous. The passage measures the opposite outcome at Odren, and paragraph 4's point is that the petrels are what keep making the soil, not that they made it once.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude to Ruhe's case that the rock settles the question?

options.text: The writer shares Ruhe's view that an island's future is fixed in the first winter after it surfaces.
The writer treats Ruhe's insistence on cementation as a blind spot that the survey record has demolished.
The writer reads the Sarnhold record as broadly bearing Ruhe out, with the bare interior a small qualification.
The writer allows that nothing lives on an uncemented island, but withholds the conclusion Ruhe builds on it.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / attitude), edge position 5. WHY-KEY (D): the concession is made in the text's own voice and is unqualified — 'nothing colonizes a shoal, and an uncemented island never gets an ecology to lose' — and it is immediately fenced: 'But cementation is a fact about the shore rather than the surface', followed by Kelvain's armored rim over a bare interior. The writer takes Ruhe's premise and refuses his conclusion that biology is downstream of the rock 'and always will be'. WHY-NOT-A (trap: role_or_attribution_swap — the TYPE-005 signature): Ruhe's quoted line is the most memorable sentence in the passage, and a solver reading for tone rather than for who is speaking hands it to the writer. The passage frames it as his position and answers it in the next breath. WHY-NOT-B (trap: polarity overshoot): dismissal overshoots a text that grants Ruhe a real point in its own voice; 'demolished' is contradicted by the concession, and nothing in the piece calls his position a blind spot. WHY-NOT-C (trap: direction reversal, hedged in form): written to sound as measured as the key, so that reaching for the cautious option decides nothing here. It fails on direction and on weight — the bare interior is not a small qualification but the observation the writer uses to bound Ruhe's claim, and the surviving flora sits in two hectares of ninety, which is the passage's evidence against biology being downstream of the rock.

generator_meta.topic: how new volcanic islands are colonized, and why a cumulative arrival list hides the turnover
